articles.title: How Does External Traffic Reach Your Pods? Kubernetes Ingress Explained
articles.excerpt: Your application works perfectly inside Kubernetes. Its Service is healthy, and the Pods are running. But when someone opens your website from the internet, how does that request find the correct appl…
articles.body: Your application works perfectly inside Kubernetes. Its Service is healthy, and the Pods are running. But when someone opens your website from the internet, how does that request find the correct application? Kubernetes Ingress provides the routing rules—but an Ingress controller makes them work. Let's follow an external HTTP/HTTPS request into a Kubernetes cluster, explore how traffic reaches the backend Pods, and troubleshoot the path when something goes wrong. 1. Where Does Ingress Fit? Imagine hosting two applications in the same cluster: shop.example.com — an online store. api.example.com — a backend API. Each application has its own Kubernetes Service. Ingress lets you define rules that route requests to the appropriate Service based on hostnames and URL paths.
articles.author: Sreekanth Kuruba

articles.title: Trust, but Verify: Setting Boundaries for AI in Your Dev Workflow
articles.excerpt: AI Ethics for Developers: 7 Principles to Follow When Building with AI It’s 5:40 on a Thursday. You’re trying to finish a search endpoint before the weekend, so you ask your AI assistant for a quick i…
articles.body: AI Ethics for Developers: 7 Principles to Follow When Building with AI It’s 5:40 on a Thursday. You’re trying to finish a search endpoint before the weekend, so you ask your AI assistant for a quick implementation. In seconds, you get clean, readable code. It runs. The tests you wrote pass. You merge it. Two weeks later, a teammate notices something odd in the logs. The assistant built the SQL query by concatenating the user’s input into a string. Your happy-path tests never tried anything hostile, so nothing caught it. Nobody was malicious here, and the tool wasn’t broken. The code looked right, it came fast, and the process skipped the part where a human asked, “What could go wrong?” That gap is what this article is about.
articles.author: DythonAI

articles.title: Embedded GUI Design: A Practical Integration Checklist for Firmware Engineers
articles.excerpt: A firmware engineer finishes integrating a display module. The hardware works. Communication is stable. But when the first operator sits down with the device, they hesitate, press the wrong button, an…
articles.body: A firmware engineer finishes integrating a display module. The hardware works. Communication is stable. But when the first operator sits down with the device, they hesitate, press the wrong button, and then ask, "Where do I confirm?" The screen is functional. The interface is not. That gap between a working display and a usable interface is where GUI design lives — and for firmware engineers, it is an integration problem as much as a design problem. GUI design is the discipline of structuring and presenting interactive elements on a screen so users can operate a system accurately and efficiently. In embedded and industrial contexts, a display that passes electrical testing can still cause operator errors, slow commissioning, and costly retraining.

articles.title: Percent Change, Explained: The Math Behind Increases, Decreases, and the 10% Trap
articles.excerpt: Percentages are everywhere — sale tags, tip screens, pay raises, stock charts. And yet the single most useful percentage skill is one almost nobody practices deliberately: percent change. Once you und…
articles.body: Percentages are everywhere — sale tags, tip screens, pay raises, stock charts. And yet the single most useful percentage skill is one almost nobody practices deliberately: percent change . Once you understand it, you can see through misleading sales, decode a raise offer in seconds, and never get tripped up by the famous "10% trap" again. The One Formula You Need Percent change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. The sign tells you the direction: positive means increase, negative means decrease. A $30 book now costs $39 → (39 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = 30% increase . A $50 sweater marked down to $38 → (38 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = −24% , i.e., a 24% decrease . That's it. Every example below is just this formula wearing a different outfit.

articles.body: 6 Min Read Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space.
